title: World Bank approves $300 million to improve primary education
excerpt: The IDA credit backs the government's Fifth Primary Education Development Programme, with a focus on reading, numeracy and children who fall behind.
content:
The World Bank’s Board of Executive Directors on Friday, 6 November, approved $300 million (about Tk 3,736 crore) for primary education in Bangladesh, The Daily Star reported on 7 November.

The money will fund the Learning Enhancement and Acceleration in Primary Education Program, which supports the government’s Fifth Primary Education Development Programme. The World Bank says it will reach about 2.6 crore (26 million) children through better classrooms, learning materials and school uniforms.

What it pays for

  • A basic literacy and numeracy package: teaching materials, structured lesson plans and teacher training.
  • Leadership training for headteachers in 90% of government primary schools, and stronger school management systems.
  • Extra help for children who fall behind, focused on the districts with the weakest results.
  • Better use of budgets and data in running schools, and stronger pre-primary education.

The credit comes from the International Development Association (IDA), the World Bank’s fund for lower-income countries, with a 25-year term that includes a five-year grace period.

The problem it targets

About half of 10-year-olds in Bangladesh cannot read a simple text suitable for their age, the report said, citing World Bank figures. Two days before the approval, the government set aside Tk 41,090 crore for digital and needs-based classrooms and school uniforms.

“Quality primary education is one of the building blocks for a globally competitive workforce,” said Jean Pesme, World Bank division director for Bangladesh and Bhutan. Tashmina Rahman, the programme’s team leader, said: “Strong foundational learning is a critical step towards the accumulation of skills for better jobs.”

Why it matters

Education NGOs that run pre-primary centres, remedial classes or teacher training in low-performing districts may find partnership openings as the programme rolls out. The focus on districts with the weakest results also gives a clear signal of where government and donor money will go.

What to watch

Which districts are chosen for remedial support, and whether NGO schools, which also teach many primary-age children, are included in the programme.

Sources

  • World Bank approves $300 million to improve Bangladesh’s primary education, The Daily Star, 7 November 2026
